text: Best in light, sandy or free-draining soil, provided the ground is not very acid or subject to prolonged waterlogging in winter. They will grow in most climates and are useful for breaking up heavy land, but they perform poorly in very heavy boulder clay unless the soil is improved.
Choose light, free-draining, non-acid soil; improve heavy clay and avoid waterlogging.
Dig the bed deeply in autumn and incorporate plenty of compost or well-rotted manure. A pH around 6.5 is suitable, so lime if necessary.
Dig deeply in autumn, add compost or manure, and lime to about pH 6.5 if needed.
A pH around 6.5 is suitable, so lime if necessary.

Good drainage is essential. Asparagus prefers a sunny, sheltered site in light, well-drained loam or sandy soil enriched with plenty of compost or well-rotted manure. Lime if the soil is very acid; a pH around 6.5 is suitable.
Choose a sunny, sheltered, well-drained bed; enrich it and lime very acid soil.

In autumn, dig or fork the bed deeply and incorporate organic matter. A dressing of lime, rock phosphate, wood ash or a general fertilizer can be useful where the soil needs it, but plenty of good compost is the main improvement. Leave the soil rough over winter and rake it down before planting.
Asparagus prefers a sunny, sheltered site in light, well-drained loam or sandy soil enriched with plenty of compost or well-rotted manure. Lime if the soil is very acid; a pH around 6.5 is suitable.
A slightly acid to neutral soil is suitable; a pH of about 6 is ideal.
Aim for slightly acid to neutral soil, ideally around pH 6.

Broad beans prefer rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining soil, and they cope better with strong or heavy ground than many other beans. Avoid waterlogged ground and very acid soil; a pH around 6.5 is ideal, so lime in winter if the soil is much below this.
Use rich, moisture-retentive, free-draining soil around pH 6.5; avoid waterlogging.
They do cope better with strong or heavy ground than many other beans. Avoid waterlogged ground and very acid soil; a pH around 6.5 is ideal, so lime in winter if the soil is much below this.

French beans do best in a warm, sheltered, sunny position and in lightish, well-drained soil improved with plenty of compost or well-rotted manure. They dislike heavy clay, cold wet ground and acid soil; a pH around 6.5 is ideal, so lime only if the soil is too acid.
Choose warm, sheltered, sunny, well-drained soil; avoid cold clay and acid ground.

They like lightish, well-drained soil improved with plenty of compost or well-rotted manure. They dislike heavy clay, cold wet ground and acid soil; a pH around 6.5 is ideal, so lime only if the soil is too acid.

Runner beans need a sheltered, sunny site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. They are not happy in hungry, badly-drained or very acid ground; a pH around 6.5 is suitable, so lime in late winter if necessary.
Choose a sunny, sheltered site with rich, moist, free-draining soil around pH 6.5.
They are not happy in hungry, badly-drained or very acid ground; a pH around 6.5 is suitable, so lime in late winter if necessary.
Dig the soil in autumn and incorporate compost or well-rotted manure if available. Like other beet crops, leaf beet prefers soil around pH 6.5, so lime if necessary.
Dig in autumn, add compost or manure, and lime to about pH 6.5 if needed.

Yellowing between leaf veins can indicate a nutrient problem, but symptoms overlap. Check soil pH and growing conditions before treating. Manganese becomes less available in alkaline soil; avoid unnecessary liming and obtain a soil test if symptoms persist.
Check drainage and soil pH; avoid over-liming and confirm the cause.
Beetroot does badly in very acid ground and prefers soil around pH 6.5, so lime if necessary. Rake in a general fertilizer 2-3 weeks before sowing if the soil is poor.
Lime acid soil to about pH 6.5 and fertilise poor ground before sowing.

Leaves wilt in summer and the tops of the roots develop brown, sunken patches. A cut root reveals blackened areas within the flesh. The cause is boron deficiency, and attacks are worst on light, over-limed land in a dry season. Confirm boron deficiency and check soil pH and moisture before acting. Existing damaged roots will not recover; obtain advice on an organic-compatible correction if a shortage is confirmed. Maintain steady soil moisture, improve soil with mature compost and avoid unnecessary liming. Do not apply borax by guesswork: the margin between deficiency and toxic excess is narrow. Correct confirmed boron deficiency carefully; avoid overdosing. Blackened roots Confirm boron shortage; seek organic correction advice.

Yellow patches develop between the veins, and in a severe attack the whole leaf turns yellow and then brown. The tell-tale sign is inward rolling of the leaf edges. The cause is manganese deficiency. Confirm the deficiency rather than diagnosing from leaf colour alone. Check pH, drainage and moisture, and obtain advice on an organic-compatible manganese correction if needed. Do not overlime the soil. Apply a suitable trace-element feed and avoid over-liming. Rolled leaves Confirm manganese shortage; avoid excess lime.
Confirm manganese shortage; avoid excess lime.
Broccoli is a brassica and grows best in firm, reasonably fertile soil with adequate humus. It is less demanding than cauliflower, but loose, hungry or acid ground gives poor results.
Use firm, fertile, humus-rich soil; avoid loose, hungry or acid ground.
Choose a sunny site and prepare the ground in autumn if possible. Dig deeply, add well-rotted manure or compost if the soil is poor, and lime if necessary.
Choose sun, dig deeply in autumn, add compost or manure, and lime if needed.

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather. Soil can remain infected for up to 20 years. Use clean plants and ground, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil on tools or footwear. Test before liming acid soil; this can reduce symptoms but does not clear the infection.
Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Lime if necessary. Brassicas dislike acid soil; aim for pH 6.5-7.5.
Dig deeply, add well-rotted manure or compost if the soil is poor, and lime if necessary.
Lime if the soil is acid. Like other brassicas, brussels sprouts dislike acid conditions and are prone to club root on sour ground.
Lime acid soil to reduce club root risk.

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather. Soil can remain infected for up to 20 years. Use clean plants and ground, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil on tools or footwear. Test before liming acid soil; this can reduce symptoms but does not clear the infection.
Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Lime if necessary. Brassicas dislike acid soil; aim for pH 6.5-7.5.

Cabbage is one of the most versatile brassicas, and with the right choice of variety it can provide food for much of the year. Spring cabbages give tender greens and small heads before many other vegetables are ready; summer and autumn cabbages provide fresh heads for salads, slaws and cooking; winter, savoy and red cabbages can stand or store into the colder months. The key is to match the variety to the season, because cabbage types differ in shape, texture, colour, hardiness and speed of hearting. They are greedy plants and need fertile, firm soil with a suitable pH, but they repay the space with dependable crops and, if cooked or used raw with care, much better flavour than their old reputation suggests.
Cabbages need fertile, firm soil rich in organic matter. Test soil pH before liming acid ground; unnecessary lime can make some nutrients less available.
Use fertile, firm soil; test before liming acid ground.

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather. Soil can remain infected for up to 20 years. Use clean plants and ground, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil on tools or footwear. Test before liming acid soil; this can reduce symptoms but does not clear the infection.
Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.

Boron deficiency can cause hollow stems and browning inside cabbage heads. Similar symptoms may have other causes, so confirm the problem with a soil test. Boron is less available in alkaline soils; avoid unnecessary liming and maintain organic matter.
Confirm with a soil test; avoid over-liming and use a suitable correction only as directed.
Check soil pH and confirm the cause before treating. Avoid unnecessary liming and use a suitable trace-element correction only if deficiency is confirmed.
Lime if necessary. Brassicas dislike acid soil; aim for pH 6.5-7.5.
Test soil pH before liming acid ground. Avoid unnecessary lime.

Carrots prefer to follow a crop which was manured the previous year. Do not add fresh manure just before sowing, as it encourages forked, watery roots and poor flavour. If the soil is acid, lime it in winter. Dig deeply in autumn, rake to a fine tilth before sowing, and apply a general-purpose fertilizer; phosphate, potash and wood ash are useful where the soil is short of them.
Follow a manured crop, avoid fresh manure, lime acid soil and prepare a fine seedbed.
Mix tiny seed with dry sand if this helps you sow thinly. Cover lightly with fine soil or peat-free compost; do not add lime merely to colour the seed.
Clayburn identity and symptoms, blanket feeding/liming advice, legacy cooking/freezing details and cultivar resistance/popularity claims need further evidence.
The 1.3 cm seed depth and foliage trim are retained: rounding to 1 or 1.5 cm would exceed the selected 15% tolerance. No blanket rounding of pH, temperatures or timings.
Avoid poor, dry or waterlogged ground. Test pH before liming acid soil; use an appropriate organic feed if fertility is low. Rake the settled bed and firm around transplants.
Use fertile, moist soil; test before liming and firm around transplants.

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather. Soil can remain infected for up to 20 years. Use clean plants and ground, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil on tools or footwear. Test before liming acid soil; this can reduce symptoms but does not clear the infection.
Avoid infected soil; clean tools. Test before liming; no cure.

Boron deficiency can cause hollow stems and brown curds. Confirm the cause with a soil test; maintain organic matter and avoid unnecessary liming. Use a suitable correction only as directed for a confirmed deficiency.
Test soil; avoid excess lime and correct confirmed deficiency.

Leaves are thin and strap-like. Plant growth is poor and cauliflower heads may be very small or fail to develop. It is caused by molybdenum deficiency due to acid soil. Test soil; correct acidity and confirmed deficiency.
Test soil; correct acidity and confirmed deficiency.
Lime if necessary. Brassicas dislike acid soil; aim for pH 6.5-7.5.
Where club root is a concern, avoid infected soil and use clean tools and healthy plants. Improve drainage and test soil before liming; lime reduces disease but does not cure infection.
Avoid infected soil; use clean tools and plants. Test before liming; no cure.
Avoid poor, hungry, dry or acid ground.
Test pH before liming; add an appropriate organic feed if needed. Keep the soil moist and firm around transplants.
Celery tolerates fairly acid soil and does not usually need lime. Where slugs are troublesome, check plants on mild, damp evenings and hand-pick them; encourage natural predators.
Do not lime routinely; hand-pick slugs on damp evenings and encourage predators.
A rich, well-drained soil with a pH of about 6-7 is ideal, although chicory will grow without heavy feeding if the ground is reasonably fertile.
Use rich, well-drained soil around pH 6–7, though heavy feeding is unnecessary.
A rich, well-drained soil with a pH of about 6-7 is ideal.

Use firm, sound gherkins and a tested preserving recipe, following its exact vinegar acidity, ingredient proportions, jar processing and storage instructions. The National Center for Home Food Preservation provides tested cucumber-pickle recipes. Simply covering cucumbers with warm vinegar and sealing a jar does not establish safe room-temperature storage.

Replaced incomplete warm-vinegar/airtight-jar/two-month recipe with tested-recipe guidance: acidity, proportions, processing and storage are necessary. No untested replacement quantities or shelf-life promised.
Endive will grow in most reasonably fertile soils, but it does best in a cool, moist position with plenty of humus. A neutral soil around pH 6-7 is suitable.
Use fertile, humus-rich soil in a cool, moist position around pH 6–7.
However, it does best in a cool, moist position with plenty of humus. A neutral soil around pH 6-7 is suitable.

Choose sun or light shade and well-drained ground. Kale can follow an early crop. Weed the bed, improve fertility with mature compost where needed and settle transplants securely. Avoid working wet soil; lime only if a soil test indicates a need.
Use settled, fertile, well-drained ground; firm transplants and lime only if a soil test indicates a need.

Swollen, distorted roots cause poor growth and wilting in sunshine. Club root persists in soil for many years, especially in acid conditions. Remove badly affected plants, keep infected roots out of home compost and avoid carrying affected soil to clean ground. Test soil before liming; a short rotation does not clear infection.
Avoid infected soil; clean tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Check soil pH, watering and feeding. Improve soil with mature compost and avoid excessive potassium. Seek advice on an organic-compatible magnesium correction if a shortage is confirmed.
Lime if necessary. Brassicas dislike acid soil; aim for pH 6.5-7.5.
Choose a sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil. Test soil before adding lime.
Use fertile, well-drained soil; test before liming.

Swollen, distorted roots cause poor growth and wilting in sunshine. Club root persists in soil for many years, especially in acid conditions. Remove badly affected plants, keep infected roots out of home compost and avoid carrying affected soil to clean ground. Test soil before liming; a short rotation does not clear infection.
Avoid infected soil; clean tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Check soil pH, watering and feeding. Improve soil with mature compost and avoid excessive potassium. Seek advice on an organic-compatible magnesium correction if a shortage is confirmed.
Lime if necessary. Brassicas dislike acid soil; aim for pH 6.5-7.5.
Leeks like moist but well-drained soil. Check soil pH before adding lime; the previous crop or the appearance of the soil alone is not a reliable guide.
Test soil before adding lime.
They like a moist but well-drained soil and tolerate a fairly high pH.
Test soil before adding lime; aim for fertile, well-drained ground that retains moisture.
Avoid acid soil; a pH around neutral is ideal, so lime if necessary. Heavy clay can be improved with repeated dressings of compost or manure before it becomes a reliable lettuce bed.
Lime acid soil toward neutral and improve heavy clay repeatedly with compost.
Avoid acid soil; a pH around neutral is ideal, so lime if necessary.
Choose an open, sunny, well-drained site. Incorporate well-rotted compost or manure ahead of planting and test soil pH before deciding whether lime is needed.
Add well-rotted organic matter and test before liming.
Prepare the bed ahead of planting with mature compost. Use an organic fertiliser only where soil fertility is low, following the label. Test before liming.
A pH around 6 is suitable; lime if the ground is more acid. Add well-rotted compost or manure in the previous autumn rather than fresh manure immediately before planting.
Aim for pH 6; add rotted organic matter in autumn, not fresh manure at planting.
Choose an open, sunny, well-drained site. Incorporate well-rotted compost or manure ahead of planting and test soil pH before deciding whether lime is needed.
Test the soil before deciding whether lime is needed.
Most of this group are brassicas and prefer fertile soil that is not strongly acid. Test the soil before deciding whether lime is needed. Shungiku is in the daisy family, not a brassica.
Test acid soil before liming; shungiku is not a brassica.
As brassicas, most dislike very acid soil.
Chinese cabbage in particular does not like acid conditions and benefits from a rich, humus-filled bed.

Retained genuine crop types, named Joi Choi/Red Frills/Waido and non-brassica shungiku. RHS crop-specific depths and baby/full-sized plant routes replace misleading universal minima. Chinese cabbage heads 30 cm/12 in. in 45 cm/18 in. rows; pak choi 10/20/30 cm for leaf/small/full crops. Corrected 3 cm to 1¼ in. Removed automatic liming, fixed 10 cm compost layer, unnecessary heart tying and universal leaf-radish root promise. Spring growing qualified rather than dismissed; all eight inline problems reviewed.

A neutral soil of about pH 6.5 suits parsnips. Very heavy soil, stones, lumps of fresh organic matter and compacted ground can make roots fork, while acid soil and fresh manure increase the risk of canker.
Aim for pH 6.5 and avoid stones, compaction, acid soil and fresh organic lumps.

In wet winters, heavy soils, acid soil or ground containing fresh manure, the tops of roots may develop brown or black fungal rot. Large roots suffer most, though there is often plenty of sound root below the damaged crown. Choose resistant varieties, lime acid soil, avoid fresh manure, and consider a later sowing for smaller, cleaner roots. Use resistant varieties, lime acid soil, avoid manure and sow later.

Peas dislike acid soil. Aim for a pH of about 6.5 or slightly above; lime if the soil is too acid. Wood ash, rock phosphate or other balanced mineral additions can be useful where the soil is deficient.
Lime acid soil to about pH 6.5 and add minerals only where deficient.

Potatoes prefer slightly acid conditions and should not be limed. Scab is encouraged by alkaline, dry soil; acidity reduces it. Potash is important for good crops, while nitrogen is useful but less critical where compost or manure has been added.
Keep soil slightly acid, never lime, and supply potash for good crops.

Common scab causes corky skin patches and is favoured by dry conditions as tubers form, particularly in alkaline soil. Avoid liming immediately before potatoes, incorporate mature compost and maintain steady moisture.
Avoid liming; keep soil moist as tubers form.
Potatoes prefer slightly acid conditions and should not be limed.
Scab is encouraged by alkaline, dry soil; acidity reduces it. Potash is important for good crops, while nitrogen is useful but less critical where compost or manure has been added.
Like most brassicas they dislike acid soil, so lime if necessary. Well-drained soil with humus is useful, especially for winter radishes and mooli.
Lime acid soil and provide humus-rich drainage, especially for winter radishes.

As brassicas, radishes dislike acid soil. Lime if needed, especially where winter radishes are to stand for longer. Apply lime where needed, especially for winter radishes. Plants grow poorly in acid soil. Test soil; lime only where needed.
Poor growth in acid soil.
Test soil; lime only where needed.
The plant is quite tolerant of soil, including slightly acid ground, and should not be limed routinely. It responds strongly to organic matter and spring moisture.
Do not lime routinely; feed generously with organic matter and spring moisture.
Aim for slightly acid to neutral soil, about pH 6–7. Test before liming, and avoid fresh or lumpy organic matter immediately before sowing.
Aim for pH 6–7; test before liming and avoid fresh manure.
Aim for slightly acid to neutral soil, about pH 6–7.
Test before liming and avoid fresh or lumpy organic matter just before sowing.
Improve the bed with mature compost before sowing. Test the soil before liming; use a suitable organic fertiliser only where soil fertility needs a boost.
Improve with compost; test before liming and feed organically if needed.
Use slightly acid to neutral soil, aiming around pH 6–6.5. Test before liming: excess lime can reduce manganese availability, but there is no single pH at which every soil causes deficiency.
Aim around pH 6–6.5; test before liming and avoid excess lime.

Yellowing between veins can have several causes. High pH or excess lime can reduce manganese availability. Check soil pH, roots and feeding before treating a confirmed deficiency; avoid unnecessary lime.
Leaves yellow in over-limed, high-pH soil.
Check the cause and pH; avoid further unnecessary lime.
Spinach dislikes acid soil.
Aim around pH 6–6.5 and test before liming. Excess lime may reduce manganese availability; diagnose yellowing before adding nutrients.

Corrected New Zealand spinach family and false low-oxalate claim; withdrew unverified Monnopa baby-food recommendation. Research supports boiling New Zealand spinach and discarding water. Cooking moved out of harvest. Seed shape is not a reliable season guide; duplicate Sigmaleaf merged at existing rank. Removed unsupported mildew/bolting superlatives, manganese pH threshold and contradictory dry-only watering. True-spinach thinning 8/15 cm with 3/6 in.; New Zealand plants 60 cm/2 ft in 90–120 cm/3–4 ft rows. All six meaningful problems and useful diagnostic detail retained. Follow-up producer verification supports Monnopa’s relative low-oxalate flavour trait, which is retained; the baby-food recommendation remains withdrawn.
Swedes are brassicas and like other members of the family need firm, reasonably fertile, non-acid soil with adequate drainage. A neutral or slightly alkaline soil is best; lime if the soil is acid.
Use firm, fertile, well-drained, non-acid soil; lime if needed.
Like other brassicas they need firm, reasonably fertile, non-acid soil with adequate drainage. A neutral or slightly alkaline soil is best; lime if the soil is acid.
Neutral to slightly acid soil, around pH 6.5–7, suits sweet corn. Good drainage, warmth and organic matter help the crop establish.
Aim for neutral to slightly acid soil, around pH 6.5–7.

For grilling, cut in half and coat the exposed surface with oil, pepper and sugar. Grill for 5 minutes. To stuff tomatoes, cut a lid, remove some pulp, fill with stuffing and bake. Tomatoes can also be skinned and used for stews, omelettes, sauces, soups and sandwiches. Sound home-grown tomatoes can be bottled using a tested preserving recipe. Follow its specified acidification and heat-processing instructions exactly.

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates. Keep soil or compost evenly moist, especially as fruit swells; avoid root damage and excessive feeding. Diagnose soil conditions before adding lime or nutrients.

Older leaves may yellow between green veins, sometimes developing brown areas. Check watering, roots, soil pH and feeding before treating a confirmed deficiency. Excess potassium can reduce magnesium uptake. Use balanced nutrition and seek advice on a suitable organic-compatible magnesium amendment if needed.
Check watering, pH and feed; avoid excess potash.

Replaced routine soil sterilisation, small 9-inch final pots, imprecise feed prescriptions, watering-for-flavour stress, premature stopping and obsolete foliage/ripening methods. Mainstream 45–60 cm/18–24 in. plant spacing and pots at least 30 cm/12 in.; cordons stop at four outdoor or about seven indoor trusses. Corrected 19°C/65°F mismatch to 66°F without percentage-rounding temperatures. Bottling is possible with tested acidification and processing; withdrew false home-grown prohibition. All distinct inline problems reviewed, duplicate greenhouse aphid/whitefly row merged and shared refs cleared without changing shared Trouble files.
Sweetness may be disappointing in wet summers. Fruit flavour improves as acidity becomes balanced by sweetness, then softens if the fruit is left extra ripe.

Turnips are brassicas and need firm, non-acid soil with reasonable drainage. A neutral or slightly alkaline soil is best; lime if the soil is acid.
Use firm, well-drained, non-acid soil; lime if needed.
They need firm, non-acid soil with reasonable drainage. A neutral or slightly alkaline soil is best; lime if the soil is acid.
